records.text: The Stratos Artificial Intelligence Data Center will cover more than 40,000 acres across three sites in Box Elder County, Utah.
records.speaker: The Guardian

appearances.snippet: The Stratos Artificial Intelligence Data Center footprint will cover more than 40,000 acres over three sites in Box Elder County in northwestern Utah.

verification.notes: Box Elder County states that the proposed Stratos project area comprises three separate areas totaling about 40,000 acres of private land plus about 1,200 acres of military and state land.

sources.title: Box Elder County Stratos Project FAQ
sources.relevance: Official county page states the project has three separate areas totaling about 40,000 acres plus state and military land.

records.text: The Stratos facility will require about nine gigawatts of power, more than Utah currently consumes.
records.speaker: The Guardian

appearances.snippet: The facility will require about nine gigawatts of power, which is more than the entire state of Utah currently consumes.

verification.notes: Current project reporting and county materials describe a full-build target of up to 9 GW. Contemporary comparisons put Utah average electricity demand near 4 GW, so the proposed capacity and consumption exceed current statewide use.

sources.title: Utah approved data center power and size report
sources.relevance: Reports the 9 GW full-build figure and compares it with current Utah electricity consumption.

records.text: The Stratos facility will consume significant water in an area affected by severe drought in recent years.
records.speaker: The Guardian

appearances.snippet: And it's going to suck up a significant amount of water in an area that has been hit by severe drought in recent years.

verification.notes: The project has sought roughly 1,911 acre-feet of water rights in drought-affected Hansel Valley, supporting concern about significant water use. However, the county says closed-loop cooling and brackish water are planned, environmental permits remain pending, and actual consumption is not yet established.

sources.title: Box Elder County Stratos Project FAQ
sources.relevance: Official county page projects 3,500 acre-feet in phase one, requires closed-loop cooling, and notes water permits and engineering reviews remain pending.

sources.title: Salt Lake Tribune: Stratos still faces public review
sources.relevance: Reports water-right applications in drought-affected Hansel Valley and unresolved permitting.

records.text: Box Elder County commissioners approved the Stratos project despite thousands of objections from Utah residents.
records.speaker: The Guardian

appearances.snippet: Last week, the project was approved by the county's commissioners despite thousands of objections lodged by Utah residents.

verification.notes: Commissioners unanimously consented to creation of the MIDA project area amid nearly 4,000 objections. The county emphasizes that this was not full construction approval and that environmental and building permits remain required, so saying the project itself was approved is overbroad.

sources.title: Box Elder County Stratos Project FAQ
sources.relevance: Official county page says commissioners consented to a project area but did not grant full construction approval, and reviewed over 2,500 public comments.

sources.title: Utah Stratos opposition and approval report
sources.relevance: Reports nearly 4,000 objections while describing the county vote.

records.text: The Stratos project will deliver thousands of jobs.
records.speaker: Kevin O'Leary

appearances.snippet: O'Leary (Kevin O'Leary) has claimed that Stratos will deliver thousands of jobs.

verification.notes: Official county forecasts project thousands of temporary construction jobs and 1,000 to 2,000 permanent jobs, confirming the prediction was made. Full construction is not approved and the jobs have not yet been delivered, so the future outcome cannot yet be verified.

records.text: Most protesters against the Stratos project do not live locally and were paid to object.
records.speaker: Kevin O'Leary

appearances.snippet: O'Leary (Kevin O'Leary) has claimed in social media posts that most of the protesters don't live locally and have been paid to object to the project.

verification.notes: Transcript context attributes this to Kevin OLeary. Public reporting confirms he alleged opponents were out-of-state and paid, but no evidence was offered and no reliable source substantiates that most protesters were nonlocal or compensated.
